opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really hard problem, and I'm not sure anyone has a great answer yet. The basic challenge is that if you have a requirement like "a human has to be in the loop for certain decisions" or "a human has to be accountable for what this firm does," there's a strong competitive pressure to make that human involvement more and more nominal. You end up with a person rubber-stamping things they don't really understand, because the AI-run parts of the system are moving much faster than any human can follow. So even within a single country, enforcement is tricky, and internationally it's harder still, because any jurisdiction that relaxes the rule gets a competitive advantage.

I think the analogies people reach for are things like nuclear nonproliferation or financial regulation, where you have some international coordination, some monitoring, and some ability to cut off access to the global system if you don't comply. With finance, for example, if you want to plug into the international banking system you have to meet certain standards, know-your-customer rules, and so on. You could imagine something similar where, if you want your AI-run firm to trade with or operate in major economies, you have to demonstrate that there's meaningful human oversight, with real auditing of what that oversight consists of, not just a checkbox.

But I'd be honest that it only works if the major players, mainly the countries with the most compute and the leading labs, actually agree it's in their interest. Compute is probably the most tractable lever, since it's concentrated and somewhat trackable. Still, I think the deeper issue is that "human involvement" is hard to define in a way that doesn't either become meaningless or become so burdensome that people route around it. So I'd focus less on a blanket rule and more on specific, high-stakes decision points where you really want human accountability, and on building tools that make it feasible for humans to understand what the AI systems are doing. If oversight is cheap and actually useful, it's much easier to sustain than if it's purely a tax imposed from outside.

r001.rationale: The response says enforcement depends on agreement among major players, especially countries with the most compute; it does not identify agreement by every country.

r002.rationale: It mentions leading labs alongside major countries, but does not identify agreement across all model infrastructure or model providers as an alternative route.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I mean, I think the honest answer is that it's really hard, and I don't think anyone has a fully worked out plan. But let me try to break it down a bit.

So first, I think you have to separate two questions: what's the actual requirement, and then how do you verify compliance. On the first one, "keep humans in the loop" is kind of underspecified. Does that mean a human has to sign off on every decision, which is obviously impractical once you have a firm running mostly on AI? Or does it mean something more like there's a human who's legally accountable, who has the authority to shut things down, and who actually understands what the organization is doing at some level of abstraction? I think the second version is more realistic, and it's closer to how we treat corporations today. We already have this concept of a board, officers, fiduciary duty. You could imagine extending that so that the humans with those roles have specific obligations around oversight of the AI systems that are doing the actual work.

Now on enforcement internationally, I think the realistic path looks less like a treaty with inspectors and more like how we handle financial regulation or anti-money laundering. Nobody can force a country to adopt these rules, but if the major economies all require it, and if you can't do business in those markets without demonstrating compliance, then you get pretty broad adoption. Firms that want access to US or EU customers, or want to be listed on exchanges, or want to use the banking system, have to meet the standard. That's a softer form of enforcement but it's actually been fairly effective in other domains.

The harder part is verification. If the requirement is just "a human exists who's nominally in charge," that's trivially gameable. You can have a figurehead who rubber-stamps everything. So I think the interesting technical and institutional question is, can you actually audit whether oversight is meaningful? Things like, are there records of the human actually reviewing significant decisions, are there interventions, does the human have the ability to understand what's happening. And this connects to interpretability and to logging and to the kind of infrastructure you'd want anyway for safety reasons.

There's also a compute angle. Right now the frontier models require a lot of compute, and that compute is concentrated in a relatively small number of places. So there's some leverage there. You could tie access to the biggest models, or to the chips, to compliance with these kinds of governance requirements. That doesn't last forever, because the cost of a given capability level keeps falling, but it buys you some time.

And I'd say the thing I worry about most isn't really enforcement against a rogue firm in a non-cooperating country. It's more that the competitive pressure erodes the requirement even among the countries that nominally agree with it. If a firm with less human oversight can move faster and make more money, there's going to be pressure to water down what "human involvement" means until it's basically nothing. So you'd want some way to make the requirement self-reinforcing, like making the humans genuinely liable, so that there's an incentive to actually pay attention rather than to just sign off. I think that's the piece that would make it stick, more than any international enforcement mechanism per se.

r001.rationale: The response proposes adoption by major economies and market-access rules, but does not identify agreement by every country as a route.

r002.rationale: The response suggests tying access to the biggest models or chips to compliance, but does not identify agreement across all model infrastructure or providers.

astra-6.text:
I think you’d probably have to enforce it through the jurisdictions where those firms operate. Even if a company is running its AI somewhere else, it still wants to sell products, have bank accounts, and enter into contracts. Those give governments some ability to require human oversight as a condition of doing business.

The harder question is what “keeping humans involved” actually means. If there’s a human who clicks approve on everything the AI proposes, that doesn’t seem to accomplish much. You’d want humans who understand the important decisions and have the authority and practical ability to intervene. And that’s much harder to verify than whether there’s a person with a particular title.

So I could imagine an international agreement around some minimum requirements, implemented through domestic law and audits. But I’m not sure how robust that would be if the AI is doing essentially all the work and the humans can’t really evaluate it. You’d need to figure out what meaningful human control looks like before you could enforce it.

r001.rationale: The response suggests an international agreement, but does not say that every country would need to agree.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify agreement across model infrastructure or model providers as an alternative route.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you’d have to make that requirement more concrete. If it’s just that a human has to sign off on decisions, you could end up with someone rubber-stamping everything the AI proposes. That doesn’t necessarily give you meaningful human control.

You’d want to specify which decisions humans have to understand and be responsible for, and what ability they need to have to intervene. Then enforcement could involve auditing firms and holding the people running them accountable. Internationally, you could imagine countries making those requirements a condition of operating in their markets.

But I don’t think there’s an easy solution. As the systems become more capable, it may get increasingly difficult to distinguish a human actually running the firm from a human nominally supervising it. So I’d be more optimistic about enforcing particular, observable constraints than a general requirement that humans remain in charge.

r001.rationale: The response suggests countries could impose the requirements as a condition of market access, but does not identify agreement by every country as an enforcement route.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention agreement across model infrastructure or model providers as an alternative route.
